title: Thunder on Sinai (Exodus 19)
hookLine: smoke, trumpet, trembling mountain, and a people at the foot

lines: THE THIRD MONTH OUT OF EGYPT.
cards: In the third month out of Egypt, the people pitch their tents at the foot of a mountain in the desert. They've seen a sea open. They've eaten bread that fell with the dew.
Moses goes up and comes down, carrying messages. Wash your clothes. Get ready.
In three days something is going to happen. Put a boundary around the mountain, and don't touch it. On the morning of the third day, it starts: thunder, lightning, a cloud sitting heavy on the peak.
Then a sound you wouldn't expect from a mountain: a trumpet, louder and louder. The whole camp trembles.

teach.b: The King James Bible tells it like this: "there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud; so that all the people that was in the camp trembled."
Then the mountain itself: "mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire," and "the whole mount quaked greatly." Smoke like a furnace. A trumpet with no trumpeter.
Before a single law is given, the people feel how big the One speaking is. Awe comes first. But it isn't only terror.

Just before the thunder, God sends Moses down with a gentle message, remembering "how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself." And a promise: you'll be a kingdom of priests, a holy nation.
A whole people, not just a few, set apart. The mountain shakes, but the voice has already said why they're here: unto myself. Where is Sinai?
Honestly, nobody knows for sure. Christian tradition points to a peak in the south of the Sinai Peninsula, with an old monastery at its foot. Others have proposed other mountains.
The Bible sometimes calls it Horeb, and never pins it to a map. For Christians, this mountain echoes forward. Jewish tradition remembers the giving of the law at the feast of Shavuot.
In Greek that feast is called Pentecost, and in the book of Acts, on the day of Pentecost, the Spirit comes with wind and fire.

how: Christians read Exodus 19 as the prelude to the Ten Commandments, and some churches read it at Pentecost, whose story in Acts takes place on the Jewish feast of Shavuot, remembered in Jewish tradition as the time the law was given at Sinai.

games.q: you're camped at the foot of the mountain. it's smoking, the ground is shaking, and a trumpet is blaring with no one blowing it. what do you do?
o: climb up for a closer look.
stay at the boundary, and tremble.
pack up and head back to Egypt.
games.why: the people stay at the foot and tremble. the boundary was there on purpose: the scene is built to make them feel how great the One speaking is.

practice: Picture the biggest thing you've ever stood near, a mountain range, the ocean at night, a sky so full of stars it made you dizzy, and put yourself back at its foot.

Notice how small you are next to it; some people find that smallness a relief, like being the right size. If you pray, you can stand before God in that smallness without words; if you don't, let the vastness be enough.

wordCard.voice: Sinai. The mountain in the desert where the people camped in the third month after Egypt, wrapped in smoke and thunder, where the law was given.

orig.note: Hebrew: the mountain's name. Its meaning and its place on the map are both uncertain.
